description: What technical documentation does the CRA require as evidence for an SR&ED claim? Explore our Canada FAQ on contemporaneous R&D records and logs.

body.text: CRA SR&ED technical documentation requirements oblige Canadian claimants to describe projects in Part 2 of Form T661 and keep contemporaneous records, made as work progressed, proving hypotheses were formulated, systematically tested and modified. Under the Income Tax Act, records must be kept for at least six years, and courts reject claims supported only by vague records or uncorroborated testimony.

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is the federal government's primary statutory instrument for stimulating private-sector research, experimental engineering, and technological innovation, delivering $4.2 billion annually in federal tax support alongside substantial provincial and territorial co-incentives1. Governed primarily by subsection 248(1), section 37, section 127, and section 127.1 of the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and sections 2900, 2902, and 2903 (as well as Part XI) of the Income Tax Regulations, the program operates through a two-part statutory mechanism: first, an immediate 100% income tax deduction (or indefinite carryforward) for allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures pooled under subsection 37(1); and second, a federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated on qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) at either an enhanced rate of 35% or a basic rate of 15%3.

Between December 2024 and October 2026, Canada’s R&D tax framework underwent its most significant legislative and administrative overhaul in over a decade10. Enacted through Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, following policy announcements in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget, Parliament enacted four structural expansions applying to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and, for capital and lease expenditures, to property acquired or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024)2:

items: Doubling of the Enhanced Expenditure Limit: The annual expenditure ceiling eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (surpassing the $4,500,000 interim proposal in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), allowing qualifying corporations to earn up to $2,100,000 annually in refundable federal tax credits on current expenditures2.

Expansion of Phase-Out Thresholds and Gross Revenue Election: For Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range expanded from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million3. Furthermore, CCPCs may now elect under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) to determine their expenditure limit reduction using a three-year average annual gross revenue threshold ($15 million–$75 million) under subsection 127(10.6) rather than taxable capital employed in Canada3.

Extension of the 35% Refundable Rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Qualifying public corporations meeting the statutory definition of an ECPC under subsection 127(9) may now claim the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures, subject to a three-year average annual gross revenue phase-out between $15 million and $75 million under subsections 127(10.6) to 127(10.64)3.

Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs: Reversing the post-2013 repeal of capital expenditure eligibility, depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (under reinstated paragraph 37(1)(b)), first-term and second-term Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) (under subsection 127(9)), and qualifying equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, once again qualify for SR&ED tax incentives7.

body.text: Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322) providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within an eight-week service standard and cutting post-filing expenditure review timelines in half, from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days2. At the provincial level, Québec abolished eight legacy innovation tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T), which provides 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on the excess18. Similarly, British Columbia’s Budget 2026 eliminated the 2027 sunset clause on the 10% BC SR&ED tax credit (Form T666), making the credit permanent while restoring capital expenditure eligibility and expanding refundable credit access to ECPCs22.
1. Legislative & Regulatory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Primary Statutory Authorities and Governing Ministries

The legal authority for Canada’s federal R&D tax incentive regime is divided between legislative policy formulation under the Department of Finance Canada and statutory administration under the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)2. Unlike jurisdictions that bifurcate R&D certification between a science ministry and a revenue authority, the CRA exercises exclusive federal administration over both the scientific and technological eligibility review (conducted by Research and Technology Advisors) and the financial audit (conducted by Financial Reviewers) of SR&ED claims17. Meanwhile, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) and the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) deliver direct innovation grants and contribution programs—most prominently the NRC Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—which interact directly with the SR&ED tax regime as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d)24. Small businesses represent the core participant base of the federal SR&ED program, accounting for 64% of all claims filed (receiving approximately $1.5 billion in support) in 2024–2025 and 65% of all claims submitted in the 2025–2026 fiscal year2.

Every federal SR&ED claim is governed by four interlocking pillars of the Income Tax Act (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). First, subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development," setting out the substantive technical criteria for basic research, applied research, experimental development, and eight permitted categories of support work, alongside seven enumerated exclusions11. Second, section 37 governs the computation of the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada under subsection 37(1) (and permissible salary or wages for SR&ED carried on outside Canada under subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2)), the annual election between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) and subsection 37(10), limitations on specified employee remuneration under subsections 37(9), 37(9.1), and 37(9.2), loss restriction event streaming rules under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1), and mandatory reporting deadlines under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12)5.

Third, section 127 and section 127.1 govern the computation of the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" and "qualified expenditures" (subsection 127(9)), the deduction of non-refundable ITCs against Part I tax payable (subsection 127(5)), the 20% supplementary ITC enhancement for CCPCs and ECPCs (subsection 127(10.1)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and phase-out formulas (subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.64)), available-for-use timing rules (subsection 127(11.2)), non-arm's-length cost adjustments (subsections 127(11.5) and 127(11.6)), reductions for assistance and contract payments (subsections 127(18) to 127(20)), unpaid current expenditure adjustments (subsection 127(26)), ITC recapture rules (subsections 127(27) to 127(36)), and refundable ITC entitlements (subsections 127.1(1) to 127.1(3))3. Fourth, sections 2900, 2902, and 2903 (and Part XI) of the Income Tax Regulations prescribe the regulatory rules for Traditional Method overhead (subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount calculation, salary base exclusions, specified employee caps, and the overall PPA cap (subsections 2900(4) to 2900(10)), Prescribed Depreciable Property exclusions (subsection 2900(11)), prescribed excluded expenditures (section 2902), and special-purpose buildings (section 2903)5.
1.2 Summary of the 2025–2026 Legislative Modernization (Bill C-15)

Following legislative proposals introduced in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and expanded in the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget (which committed an additional ongoing investment of $440 million projected to generate $1.2 billion annually in economic output), Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 20262. Between May and October 2026, the CRA published revised editions of Form T661 (May 15, 2026), Form T1145 (May 15, 2026), Schedule T2SCH31 (May 22, 2026), and Schedule T2SCH49 (May 29, 2026), alongside updated administrative policies to align with the enacted legislation13.

body.text: 2. Substantive Technical Eligibility: Subsection 248(1) & CRA Guidelines
2.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of three core research categories or a fourth derivative category of eligible support work29. Paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research) encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view30. Basic research aims solely to expand the existing scientific knowledge base—such as theoretical physics experiments demonstrating the existence and measuring the mass and charge of elementary particles like the electron, or laboratory characterization of a newly discovered virus—and is frequently conducted by universities, research institutes, or biotechnology and nanotechnology enterprises30.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view30. For example, a private corporation investigating the properties of semiconductors and how electrons behave within them in hopes of eventually creating a semiconductor amplifier (the principle of the transistor) is conducting applied research even before any physical device or prototype is fabricated36. Paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development)—which represents the most commonly claimed category of SR&ED in Canada—comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto30. Experimental development seeks to generate or discover technological knowledge or know-how when existing engineering knowledge is insufficient to overcome system-level constraints or technical problems, such as scaling up and optimizing a manufacturing process30.

Finally, paragraph 248(1)(d) (Support Work) includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada30. Support work is never SR&ED on its own; computer programming, engineering design, or testing only qualifies to the extent that it was carried out specifically to perform and directly support eligible core research or experimental development undertaken in Canada30.
2.2 Statutorily Excluded Activities (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))
Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes work with respect to seven enumerated categories—collectively referred to as excluded work—which cannot be claimed for SR&ED tax incentives30:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion30;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes30;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities30;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas30;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process30;
Paragraph (j): Style changes30; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection30.

body.text: In administering paragraphs (e) through (k), the CRA’s Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (updated August 13, 2021) establish that exclusions should only be evaluated after it has been determined that core eligible SR&ED work exists30. The decisive factor distinguishing eligible paragraph (d) support work from excluded work is purpose—why the work was performed30. If data collection or testing is carried out to sustain product quality, verify conformity to design specifications, or support normal commercial operations, it constitutes excluded quality control or routine data collection under paragraphs (f) and (k)30. Conversely, if data collection or testing is executed specifically to test a hypothesis and directly support basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d)30. Furthermore, performing excluded work alongside eligible SR&ED—such as conducting eligible metallurgical process SR&ED while simultaneously prospecting for minerals—does not disqualify the eligible SR&ED project, provided all activities and costs relating to the excluded mineral prospecting are segregated and excluded from the claim30.
2.3 The "Two Requirements" Framework ("Why" and "How") vs. The "Five Questions"

In August 2021, the CRA replaced its archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (dated April 24, 2015) with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives30. Whereas the 2015 policy structured eligibility around the Five Questions derived from Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, the updated Guidelines present those same statutory principles of subsection 248(1) through Two Requirements—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement—which provide a common analytical language for claimants and CRA officials11.

Under the "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty), work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement11. The CRA emphasizes that advancement requires the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge (such as new theories, predictive models, or systemic technological understanding) that advances the knowledge base of science or technology, rather than merely gathering factual knowledge (such as routine measurements or empirical operational data)30. New conceptual knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning it is uncertain whether a given objective or result can be achieved due to an insufficiency or limitation in available scientific or technological knowledge (comprising both the company's internal technical resources and publicly accessible knowledge and competent professional practice)11. If a technical uncertainty is circumvented using a workaround based on existing available knowledge without attempting to resolve the underlying uncertainty, the work is ineligible30. Similarly, acquiring existing knowledge through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring external consultants or experts, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not satisfy the advancement requirement30. Crucially, technical or commercial success is irrelevant: the "Why" requirement examines strictly whether the purpose of the work was to achieve scientific or technological advancement, regardless of whether the experiment ultimately succeeded or failed30.

Under the "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search), the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis11. Merely being organized or following standard engineering design methodologies does not suffice; rather, the systematic approach requires four sequential steps11:

items: Defining the problem and generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the scientific or technological uncertainty11.
Planning and testing the hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and be modified as a result of testing11.
Developing logical conclusions based on the findings and results of the experiment or analysis11.
Keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses11.

body.text: In both CRA technical reviews and Tax Court jurisprudence, the Two Requirements map directly onto the Five Organizing Questions11:

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?11
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?11
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?11
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?11
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?11

body.text: Furthermore, in defining project boundaries on Form T661, the CRA distinguishes between a company project (which has a broad commercial objective, such as launching a commercial product or expanding a plant) and an SR&ED project (which exists as a subset of interrelated technical activities necessary to resolve specific scientific or technological uncertainties)30. An SR&ED project begins when scientific or technological uncertainties are identified and ends when the advancement is achieved (uncertainty resolved) or when it is determined that the uncertainty cannot be resolved; routine troubleshooting, debugging, fine-tuning without technological uncertainty, customer site implementation, and beta testing to verify specifications fall outside the SR&ED project boundary30.
2.4 Shop-Floor SR&ED: Production Runs and Asset Development

When experimental development is conducted in an industrial or manufacturing environment ("shop-floor SR&ED"), claimants must apply the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy30. The CRA categorizes shop-floor production trials into two distinct contexts: Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) and Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP)38.

In an ED+EP scenario, an experimental production run is required specifically to test an experimental process or material and does not take place concurrently with normal commercial production38. Under ED+EP, the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in the experimental development work resulting in the required experimental production (including non-specialized employees operating machinery required to produce the experimental run, provided they are supervised by scientific or technological staff) and the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the required trial volume are allowable SR&ED expenditures1. However, any excess production beyond the volume reasonable and necessary for the SR&ED is strictly disallowed37.

By default, if a production run required for SR&ED is not purely ED+EP, it is classified as ED+CP, where experimental development occurs simultaneously with normal commercial production on a commercial facility line38. Under ED+CP, all labour, overhead, and material costs normally incurred for standard commercial production must be excluded from the claim; only the excess incremental costs directly associated with the experimental development work—such as the transition (ramp-up) period leading into the experimental stage and the experimental development stages themselves, ending prior to the ramp-down return to standard production, plus additional input materials consumed beyond standard production norms—are allowable SR&ED expenditures38.
3. Financial Architecture: Section 37 Deduction Pool vs. Section 127 ITC Pool

A critical principle of Canadian R&D tax law is that an "SR&ED expenditure" (allowable for the Section 37 deduction pool) and a "qualified expenditure" (eligible to earn the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit) are governed by separate statutory provisions and rarely equal the same dollar amount5.
3.1 The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Subsection 37(1))

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act (calculated in Part 3, Section C of Form T661 and deducted on Line 411 of T2 Schedule 1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada accumulates allowable SR&ED expenditures in a cumulative expenditure pool6. When accounting for SR&ED on T2 Schedule 1, any SR&ED expenditures expensed on the corporation’s financial statement income statement are first added back on Line 118 of Schedule 1, and the discretionary deduction claimed from the subsection 37(1) pool (Line 460 of Form T661) is deducted on Line 411 of Schedule 141. A positive balance in the subsection 37(1) pool (Line 470 of Form T661) does not expire; the CRA treats the pool as a running balance without tracking the specific year of origin, and undeducted balances may be carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year6.

body.text: When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust experiences a new majority-interest beneficiary), a loss restriction event occurs under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1)6. A deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately prior to the acquisition of control, and the subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil unless the continuity conditions of subsection 37(6.1) are satisfied6. Under subsection 37(6.1), the undeducted pool balance accumulated prior to the acquisition of control may be reinstated, carried forward, and deducted in a subsequent taxation year only if (1) the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and (2) the deduction is limited to the corporation's income for that year (before making any subsection 37(1) deduction) derived from that same business or a similar business6. Additionally, per Section 4.0 of the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, no deduction is permitted for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED, ensuring that only the performer—and not a subsequent purchaser of intellectual property rights or foreign-developed technology—receives SR&ED tax incentives6.
3.2 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method Election

Under subsection 37(10) and clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B), a claimant must select either the Proxy Method (Line 160 of Form T661) or the Traditional Method (Line 162 of Form T661) for each taxation year when first filing Form T661 for that year5. The election is made on an annual, year-by-year basis and is irrevocable for that taxation year once Form T661 is filed; claimants cannot switch methods for a filed year by submitting an amended return, though they remain free to choose a different method in subsequent taxation years5. If a claimant does not elect the Proxy Method on Line 160, the Traditional Method applies automatically by default1.

Under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)), the claimant specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates all actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures (reported on Line 360) that are either all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) attributable, or directly attributable (directly related and incremental under Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3)), to the prosecution of SR&ED or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada5. These actual overhead expenditures are added to both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool5.

Conversely, under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)), the claimant does not track or claim actual overhead or indirect supporting salaries on Form T661 (instead deducting those actual outlays as ordinary business expenses under section 9)1. In lieu of actual overhead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), equal to 55% of the eligible salary base under Regulation 2900(4)—which is added solely to the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (Line 502 of Form T661) to earn Investment Tax Credits5.

4. Detailed Rules for Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs)
4.1 Salaries and Wages (SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy)

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I, including fees received for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business, but excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances31. Under the CRA’s SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), eligible SR&ED salary or wages include regular gross wages reported on a T4 slip, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducements or non-competition payments treated as employment remuneration, bonuses and remuneration based on profits (strictly for non-specified employees), and qualifying cash or non-cash taxable benefits under section 6 (such as automobile benefits including standby charges, housing, board and meals, gifts and awards, interest-free or low-interest loans, group term life insurance policies, and tuition fees)31. A non-cash taxable benefit may be included in SR&ED salary or wages only if (1) its value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs incurred by the employer, (2) its value excludes any Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) or Provincial Sales Tax (PST) unless no input tax credit can be claimed, and (3) the actual costs to which the non-cash benefit relates are not also claimed as a regular business expense31.
Conversely, four specific categories of employee-related outlays are statutorily excluded from SR&ED salary or wages31:

items: Employer's Share of Related Benefits: Employer contributions to payroll programs or benefit plans (such as CPP, QPP, EI, workers' compensation, or group health plans) are excluded from salary or wages, though they may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 if the Traditional Method is elected and they bear a direct link to hands-on SR&ED work31.

Extended Vacation or Sick Leave: Remuneration paid during extended vacation or extended sick leave is excluded because the employee is neither directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED nor directly engaged in SR&ED during extended absences31.
Stock Option Benefits (Section 7): Stock option benefits under section 7 are excluded because they are considered not to be an expenditure incurred by the corporation for SR&ED31.

Retiring Allowances: Excluded by the subsection 248(1) definition of salary or wages (and covered by the PPA under the Proxy Method), though potentially claimable on Line 360 as overhead under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED5.

body.text: "Directly Engaged" Salary Rules and Permissible Tasks

Under the Proxy Method, only salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (Lines 300 to 309) may be claimed5. Whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED is a question of fact based on the tasks performed and time spent rather than job titles1. Under Regulation 2900(5) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), if the portion of an employee's time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of their employment time, that portion is deemed to be 100% of their eligible salary or wages5. Eligible directly engaged tasks encompass hands-on experimentation and analysis, eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, non-specialized work (such as operating a machine for an experiment or feeding raw materials) when directly supervised by scientific or technological staff, first-line technical supervision directing the course of ongoing SR&ED or providing direct technical input (including technical input into SR&ED contract administration), technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects (assigning personnel, setting job priorities, or evaluating material quality), technological feasibility studies for carried-out SR&ED projects, and preparing internal technical documentation1. Clerical and administrative staff (such as accounting, payroll, legal support, purchasing, sales, human resources, shipping, receptionists, and secretaries) and executive managers performing non-technological decision-making above first-line supervision are not directly engaged31. Under the Traditional Method, however, clerical and administrative staff providing direct non-technological services to SR&ED employees may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead if their wages are directly related and incremental to ongoing SR&ED1.
Specified Employees (10%+ Shareholders and Non-Arm's-Length Employees)

Under subsection 248(1), a specified employee is an employee who either (1) is a specified shareholder of the employer—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time during the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of any corporation related to the employer—or (2) does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, brother, sister, or other relative of a controlling or specified shareholder under section 251)31. Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory caps:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): Under subsection 37(9), specified employees cannot include any bonus or remuneration based on profits in allowable SR&ED salary or wages11.

Section 37 Allowable Salary Cap of 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): Under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum SR&ED salary or wages of a specified employee that can be included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 305) is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee divided by 36531: A × B/365, where A is 5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year on which the employee is a specified employee of the claimant. If a specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, this 5 × YMPE limit must be shared among the associated corporations under subsection 37(9.2) using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED))31.

PPA Salary Base Cap of Lesser of 75% Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulation 2900(7) & (8)): When calculating the Proxy Method salary base in Part 5 of Form T661, a specified employee's inclusion is further restricted under Regulation 2900(7) to the lesser of 75% of their total eligible salary/wages or 2.5 × YMPE (prorated by days employed)34.

body.text: Unpaid Remuneration (180-Day Rule under Subsection 78(4))

Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year and are excluded from both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation for that year (reported on Line 315 of Form T661)4. When subsequently paid in a later taxation year, the expenditure is deemed incurred in that payment year and claimed on Line 310 of Form T661, provided it was reported on Line 315 in the year accrued34. However, under Regulation 2900(9), prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310) are permanently excluded from the PPA salary base34.
Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (10% Rule)

Under subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2), a claimant may include "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work carried on physically outside Canada (Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees), which are deemed to be expenditures made in Canada and eligible for ITCs, if all five statutory conditions are met1:

items: The SR&ED work outside Canada was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (never a contractor or subcontractor)1.
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred1.
The work was related to a business of the claimant1.
The SR&ED work performed outside Canada was an integral part of, and solely in support of, SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant1.
The salary or wages paid are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country1.

body.text: Under subsection 37(1.5), the maximum amount of permissible salary or wages for SR&ED carried on outside Canada is capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada31. Furthermore, under the Traditional Method, no SR&ED overhead or other expenditures (such as travel, hotel, or meal costs) relating to salary or wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada can be allowed under subsection 37(1)32.
4.2 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Mechanics (Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy)

For claimants electing the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is computed in Part 5 of Form T661 and transferred to Line 50234. Since 2014, subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations fixes the PPA at 55% of the salary base, subject to the overall PPA cap under Regulation 2900(6)34.

In Part 5, Section A, the claimant first computes the salary base for non-specified employees by taking total directly engaged SR&ED salaries and wages from Lines 300 and 307 (Line 810) and subtracting on Line 812 all universal exclusions mandated by Regulation 2900(9): (1) taxable benefits under section 6, (2) unpaid amounts from a prior year paid in the current year (Line 310), (3) remuneration based on profits, (4) bonuses, and (5) employer contributions to related benefits34. This yields the net non-specified employee subtotal on Line 81441.
Next, for each specified employee (Boxes 850 to 860), Regulation 2900(7) restricts the amount included in the salary base to the lesser of two amounts34:

items: 75% Limit: 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the employer for the year (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages, entered in Box 852; on Form T661, Box 852 is multiplied by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED up to a maximum of 75% in Box 854 to yield Box 856)34; or

2.5 × YMPE Limit (Box 858): Calculated using the statutory formula34: 2.5 × A × B/365 where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends ($71,300 for 2025; $74,600 for 2026) and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for time during the year that the individual was not a specified employee)34. Under Regulations 2900(8) and 2900(10), if the corporate claimant is associated with another corporation (including related individuals or partnerships with related/associated members) that employed the same specified employee in a taxation year ending in the same calendar year, the combined salary base inclusion across the associated group cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE (allocated via Form T1174)33.

body.text: Adding the total allowable specified employee salary base (Line 816) to Line 814 produces the total Salary Base (Line 818), which is multiplied by 55% on Line 82041. Finally, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA to ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specified statutory deductions do not exceed total business deductions claimed in the year34: PPA ≤ A − B − C

where A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold, summed across all businesses carried on by the claimant); B is the total deductions claimed in the year under section 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, bad debts), section 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), section 26 (banks), section 30 (improving land for farming), section 32 (insurance agent or broker), section 37 (SR&ED expenditure deduction on T2 Schedule 1 Line 411), sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and section 104 (trusts); and C is the total expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (rent)34. In general, the Overall Cap will not restrict the 55% PPA if the claimant has deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses for every $100 of eligible salary included in the salary base34.
4.3 Materials Consumed or Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) (Traditional Method), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), and Regulation 2900(2)(a), a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada41. Under the CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" refers strictly to physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or items (generally in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible "thing" (an intermediate product, by-product, or final product) on which the SR&ED is carried out, that results from the SR&ED, or that is involved in testing a new or improved process44.

Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers (including original acquisition cost plus reasonable costs to bring the item to the required condition and location, such as galvanization or freight), but can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED—not when acquired into inventory1. Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED; materials forming part of experimental production or a custom asset sold for more than 10% of the original cost are not considered consumed44. Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials that have been altered or incorporated into a prototype, custom product, or commercial asset during SR&ED and retain value (not rendered virtually valueless); if that property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the cost of the transformed materials is subject to SR&ED ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36)44. Animals and plants (along with feed, seed, growth media, agar, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides, except during simultaneous commercial production or for unmanipulated control groups) qualify as materials for SR&ED if they compose the body of the thing on which SR&ED is performed44. Conversely, laboratory supplies and items that do not compose the body of the experimental object—such as test tubes, pipettes, vials, Petri dishes, beakers, flasks, filter papers, cleaning supplies, computer discs (CDs/DVDs), general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas, propane), and processing acids, solvents, soaps, or lubricants—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED, though they may qualify as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method44.
4.4 Overhead and Other Expenditures (SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy)

Claimants electing the Traditional Method may claim SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Income Tax Regulations paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(a)–(b)32. Under the CRA’s SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), an expenditure (or reasonable portion thereof) is directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada only if it satisfies two cumulative tests32:

items: Directly Related Test: The expenditure must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform the SR&ED32.
Incremental Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred32.

body.text: While a specific portion of a variable expense (such as 25 boxes out of 100 boxes of supplies used by SR&ED staff, or 10% of variable metered electricity running experimental equipment used 10% of the time for SR&ED) meets the incremental test, a flat percentage allocation of general corporate expenses (such as claiming 25% of corporate travel expenses because 25% of employees perform SR&ED) is disallowed32. Similarly, fixed costs that do not vary with usage—such as a fixed $100,000 annual equipment maintenance contract on a machine used 40% for SR&ED and 60% for commercial production—fail the incremental test unless the claimant proves with evidence that a lower-cost contract would have been used absent the SR&ED32.

With respect to personnel and hiring costs under the Traditional Method, moving expenses (defined in subsection 62(3)) to relocate selected SR&ED candidates or transfer SR&ED employees to another facility within Canada, as well as taxable benefits to employees related to selecting and hiring SR&ED personnel (such as a taxable benefit for a housing loss under subsections 6(19) and 6(20)), qualify as SR&ED overhead if directly related and incremental5. In contrast, headhunter/recruitment agency fees, job advertising expenses, candidate interview travel costs, and immigration/work permit/visa costs are deductible only as regular business expenses and cannot be included in the Section 37 pool or earn ITCs32. A retiring allowance (defined in subsection 248(1)) paid to an SR&ED employee can be allocated to Line 360 under the Traditional Method based on the employee's historical ratio of allowed SR&ED wages to total employment wages over their career if it satisfies the directly related and incremental tests5. Finally, subparagraph 2902(a)(i) of the Income Tax Regulations designates specific outlays as "prescribed expenditures" that can never qualify for ITCs even under the Traditional Method, including general business administration or management (except eligible clerical/support wages under clause 2902(a)(i)(A)), legal or accounting fees (clause 2902(a)(i)(B)), interest and financing expenses (clause 2902(a)(i)(C) and paragraphs 20(1)(c)–(g)), and convention and conference expenses (clause 2902(a)(i)(F))4.
4.5 Subcontractors (SR&ED Contracts) and Third-Party Payments
1. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340) and the Taxable Supplier Rule

When a claimant (payer) contracts with an arm's-length performer to carry out SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), 100% of the contract cost is included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 340), and 80% is included in Section 127 qualified expenditures to earn an ITC (with the remaining 20% subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661)4. Under subsection 127(9), however, a current expenditure for an SR&ED contract is excluded from qualified expenditures (and subtracted on Line 528) if it is paid or payable to, or for the benefit of, a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier—meaning a foreign contractor that does not carry on business through a permanent establishment in Canada4. This rule prevents "double dipping": for example, if Canadian corporation K Limited pays Canadian corporation L Limited $1,000 for an SR&ED contract, and L Limited subcontracts the work to foreign non-resident F Limited (no Canadian permanent establishment) for $950, which in turn subcontracts the work to Canadian corporation M Limited for $900, the payment to L Limited is for the benefit of a non-taxable supplier, while M Limited can claim its own $850 of SR&ED costs unreduced by the payment received from non-taxable supplier F Limited4. Additionally, for expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, the former capital look-through rule under former subsections 37(14) and 37(15) no longer applies, so contract payments and third-party payments are no longer reduced by the performer's capital or equipment lease outlays8.
2. Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts (Line 345), Form T1146 Transfers, and NAL Purchases

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (Line 345), the payer's contract outlay is allowable in the payer's Section 37 deductible pool, but is excluded from the payer's Section 127 qualified expenditures under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) (Line 538)1. Simultaneously, the amount received by the NAL performer is excluded from the definition of "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), allowing the NAL performer to claim the SR&ED expenditures and ITCs directly on the underlying costs it incurred4.

Alternatively, the NAL performer (transferor) and NAL payer (transferee) may file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer qualified expenditures from the performer (Line 540) to the payer (Line 508)4. The transferable amount is limited to the least of three amounts: (1) the amount specified by the parties on Form T1146; (2) the performer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of its tax year before deducting the transfer; and (3) the total of all amounts that would be contract payments (if the parties dealt at arm's length) paid by the payer within 180 days of the performer's year-end for qualified expenditures incurred and paid by the performer within 180 days of its year-end (or transferred to the performer by another NAL party)4. If a performer attempts to transfer more than this statutory ceiling, the Act dictates that no amount can be transferred4. Partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures under Form T1146 because a partnership is not a "person" for purposes of the transfer rules4. Furthermore, when a claimant purchases goods (property) or non-SR&ED services (including post-December 15, 2024 property leases, which the Act deems to be a service based on normal accounting depreciation) from a NAL supplier, subsection 127(11.6) caps the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes at the lesser of the claimant's outlay or the adjusted selling cost / adjusted service cost to the NAL supplier (reported as an adjustment on Lines 542 and 543 of Form T661; if the NAL supplier originally received the property as a gift, its adjusted selling cost is nil)4.
3. Third-Party Payments (Line 370 and Form T1263)

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) and subsection 37(7) (Third-Party Payments Policy), claimants may claim payments made to qualifying third-party entities (Line 370)—specifically A entities (corporations resident in Canada), B to E entities (approved associations, Canadian universities and affiliated colleges [which are automatically approved], approved research institutes, non-profit SR&ED corporations, and approved granting councils), and F entities (tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j))—for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant’s business, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results1. Each payment requires a completed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) and is 80% eligible for Section 127 ITCs (20% deducted on Line 529)1. Payments in kind (property or services supplied unconditionally to a university or college) are valued at evidenced fair market value, whereas third-party payments used to acquire a building or pay building rent are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d)55. Agricultural producers contributing research check-off dues or levies through an agricultural organization acting as their agent to fund approved B, C, or D entities may claim the SR&ED percentage reported by the agricultural organization (which must file Form T661 within 6 months of its year-end)55.

body.text: 4.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (ASA ≥90% Rule – Line 390, Lines 262–263 & Part 6B)

Under reinstated paragraph 37(1)(b), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III), and the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), expenditures made after December 15, 2024, to acquire depreciable property (as defined in subsection 13(21), excluding land, inventory, goodwill, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e)) qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that either8:

items: The property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada8; or
All or substantially all (≥90%) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada8.

body.text: Capital cost includes the purchase price plus legal, accounting, engineering, installation, customs/excise duties, transportation, and significant storage costs (and for self-manufactured equipment, materials, direct labour, and overhead, excluding profit)8. While both new and used depreciable property meeting the ≥90% ASA test can be included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 390), used property (property used or acquired for use or lease for any purpose before acquisition by the claimant) is a prescribed expenditure under Income Tax Regulations paragraph 2902(b) and is excluded from Section 127 qualified expenditures (Line 530), meaning only new property can earn an ITC8. Furthermore, under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) cannot be claimed as an SR&ED capital expenditure and must be depreciated in its standard CCA class8.

An SR&ED capital expenditure deducted from the Section 37 pool is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) in a separate prescribed class; consequently, property claimed on Line 390 must not be included on Schedule 8 (T2SCH8, Capital Cost Allowance)1. If a claimant fails to claim a capital expenditure on Form T661 by the 18-month reporting deadline (subsection 37(11)), it forfeits SR&ED treatment and must depreciate the asset under standard CCA rules on Schedule 88. On the May 2026 version of Form T661, claimants must enter the names and percentage of project operating time of the 10 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED properties per project on Lines 262 and 263, and report the 20 most expensive depreciable properties across all projects in Part 6B (Boxes 780, 782, and 786)13.

Crucially, under subsections 37(1.2) and 127(11.2) (referencing the available-for-use rules in subsections 13(26) to 13(28) and 248(19)), depreciable property is deemed not to have been acquired—and capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) are deemed not to have been incurred—before the property becomes available for use by the taxpayer8. As noted in technical analyses of Bill C-15, the wording of amended subsection 127(11.2) creates a potential opportunity for ITC claims: if R&D equipment (such as an environmental test chamber) was purchased and delivered prior to December 16, 2024, but was not hooked up, commissioned, and available for use until on or after December 16, 2024, subsection 127(11.2) deems the expenditure not to have been incurred until it became available for use after December 15, 2024, potentially qualifying for Section 127 ITCs (though the CRA or Department of Finance could challenge or amend this technical interpretation)14.
2. Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE – Line 504 & Part 6C)

Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 127(9)(a)(iii) (SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, updated May 22, 2026), new depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test but is used primarily (>50% to <90% of actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada qualifies as Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), provided it is neither General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) nor Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11)16.

items: First Term SUE & Second Term SUE (25% + 25% = 50% Capital Cost Inclusion): The First Period begins when the equipment becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time16. If actual SR&ED operating time during the First Period exceeds 50%, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost (excluding borrowing costs under section 21 and adjusted for NAL transactions under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 50413. The Second Period begins when the equipment becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time; if the equipment qualified as First Term SUE and cumulative actual SR&ED operating time over the Second Period exceeds 50%, a second 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies for the ITC on Line 504 in that subsequent year13. For example, in Section 3.5 of the CRA Policy, a machine acquired on January 2, 2025, for $300,000 (with a December 31 tax year-end, running 1,300/1,600 SR&ED hours in 2025, 1,600/2,000 in 2026, and 800/2,000 in 2027) is under 12 months at December 31, 2025, and thus claims First Term SUE in its 2026 tax year (2,900/3,600 = 81% SR&ED use → $75,000 qualified expenditure) and Second Term SUE in its 2027 tax year (3,700/5,600 = 66% SR&ED use → $75,000 qualified expenditure)16.

CCA Treatment & Part 6C Reporting: The capital cost of SUE is not included in the Section 37 deductible pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the equipment under standard CCA rules on Schedule 8 (T2SCH8) and reports the 20 most expensive SUE properties in Part 6C of Form T661 (Boxes 788, 790, and 792)13.

Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) Exclusion (Regulation 2900(11)): Whereas SUE eligibility is tested on actual use during the First and Second Periods, PDP exclusion under paragraphs 2900(11)(c) and (d) is tested on intended use at the time of acquisition16. A property is disqualified as a PDP if, at acquisition, the claimant intended both (1) that it would be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility, plant, or production line, and (2) that over its expected useful life it would be used primarily (>50%) for non-SR&ED activities16.

body.text: 3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Lines 350, 355 & Part 6A)

Under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada are evaluated over the 12-month taxation year (or for a taxation year straddling December 16, 2024, as a percentage of total operating time after December 15, 2024; claimants cannot isolate a 2-to-3-month window within a 12-month year)7:

items: ASA Leased Equipment (≥90% Operating Time – Line 350): Under both the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), if leased equipment is used 90% or more of its operating time in the year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the post-December 15, 2024 lease cost is claimed on Line 350 (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method)7.

Primarily Used Leased Equipment (>50% to <90% Operating Time – Line 355 vs. Line 360): Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% (half) of the post-December 15, 2024 lease cost is claimed on Line 355 (and 0% if used ≤50% of the time)7. Under the Traditional Method, the claimant enters "0" on Line 355 and instead claims the exact proportional SR&ED usage percentage for equipment used less than 90% of the time on Line 360 as overhead, provided the lease cost is directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c))7. All project-level lease costs must be itemized in Part 6A of Form T661 (equalling the sum of Lines 350 and 355)13.

Land and Building Leases: Rent or lease payments for a building are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e) / subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i) (unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance under Regulation 2903, or a non-building structure such as a bridge or dam; mixed building-and-equipment leases must be reasonably allocated)7. Lease of land is allowable as overhead under the Traditional Method if ASA or directly attributable to SR&ED, but is completely disallowed under the Proxy Method7.

body.text: 4.7 Unpaid Current Expenditures (Subsection 127(26)), Assistance, and ITC Recapture

Under subsection 127(26), any current SR&ED expenditure other than salary or wages (such as materials, contracts, overhead, or equipment leases) that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year for Section 127 ITC purposes (subtracted on Line 520 of Form T661) and is instead added to qualified expenditures on Line 500 in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (at 80% if the unpaid outlay was an arm's-length contract or third-party payment)4.

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) (Assistance and Contract Payments Policy), both the Section 37 deductible pool (Lines 429–432) and Section 127 qualified expenditures (Lines 513–517) must be reduced on a project-by-project basis by all government assistance (grants such as NRC IRAP, subsidies, forgivable or conditional-repayment loans, GST/HST input tax credits or rebates on acquired property, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance (inducements or reimbursements included under paragraph 12(1)(x)), and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date of the return4. Assistance for one project cannot reduce expenditures of another project; if assistance exceeds a project's Section 37 pool, the project pool is reduced to nil and the excess is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (or allocated among non-arm's-length group members via Form T1145 under subsection 127(20), which may be filed by the transferor's filing due date or within the Notice of Objection period)26. When a claimant elects the Proxy Method and earns a provincial R&D tax credit (such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit), the portion of the provincial credit earned on the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) reduces federal Section 127 qualified expenditures (Line 513), but does not reduce the federal Section 37 deductible pool (Line 429) because overhead is not in the Section 37 pool under the Proxy Method; instead, the PPA-attributable provincial credit is included directly in corporate income on T2 Schedule 1 under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received26. Repayments of assistance or contract payments increase the Section 37 pool (Line 445) and earn ITCs on Line 560 at the exact rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the expenditure3.

Finally, when SR&ED property—including materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), animals/growing things, or property acquired via an SR&ED contract—is sold or converted to commercial use, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) (Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy) and subsection 37(6) trigger ITC recapture and deemed CCA recapture8:

items: SR&ED ITC Recapture (Subsections 127(27)–(36)): The recaptured ITC (equal to the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property or the applicable ITC rate multiplied by the proceeds of disposition or fair market value on conversion) is added directly to Part I tax payable for the year (or for a partnership under subsections 127(28), 127(30), and 127(31), reduces partnership ITCs first and flows any excess recapture through tiered partnerships to the partners' Part I tax)8. In the subsequent taxation year, the recaptured ITC amount is added back to the claimant's Section 37 deductible pool on Line 453 under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3)6. Under subsection 127(32), "cost" for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire tangible property from another person and excludes internal labour or overhead to modify or manufacture the property: thus, if a company pays an arm's-length supplier $12,000 to manufacture a component, the full $12,000 is subject to recapture upon sale, whereas if the company manufactures the component in-house, no recapture applies to the internal salaries or overhead—only to the cost of the transformed raw materials53.

Deemed CCA Recapture on Disposed SR&ED Capital Property: When post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED depreciable property is sold (or converted to commercial use), the lesser of the sale proceeds (or FMV) and the undeducted expenditure balance for that specific property remaining in the Section 37 pool reduces the Section 37 pool on Line 440 of Form T6618. Any excess of sale proceeds over that undeducted pool balance (up to the original capital cost) is included directly in business income as CCA recapture, and any proceeds exceeding original capital cost constitute a capital gain or income (while any loss on disposition cannot be claimed as a capital loss, instead generating a terminal loss)8. If converted to commercial use, the fair market value of the asset is also added to Schedule 8 (T2SCH8) for future regular CCA depreciation8.

5.1 Enhanced 35% vs. Basic 15% ITC Rates and the $6 Million Expenditure Limit
Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) (SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, updated October 7, 2026), federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits are earned at two statutory rates3:

items: Enhanced 35% Rate (15% Basic Rate + 20% Enhancement under s. 127(10.1)): Earned by Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit3.

Basic 15% Rate ("Specified Percentage" under s. 127(9)): Earned by CCPCs and ECPCs on qualified SR&ED expenditures exceeding their annual Expenditure Limit, and by all other corporations, individuals (sole proprietors), partnerships, and trusts on all qualified SR&ED expenditures3. (Note: Under subsection 127(9), no ITC may be earned on any expenditure incurred in the course of earning income that is exempt from Part I tax3.)

body.text: For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit is $6,000,000 (doubled from the $3,000,000 limit that applied to CCPCs for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024)3. The $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit must be shared among associated CCPCs under subsections 127(10.21), 127(10.3), and 127(10.4) using Schedule 49 (T2SCH49) or among consolidated ECPCs (members of a group preparing consolidated financial statements) under subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.64)3. The $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit phases out linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000) under two statutory methods3:

items: Taxable Capital Method for CCPCs (Subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21)): Unless a revenue election is filed, a CCPC's $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada (as defined in the Act; see archived IT-532) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,0003: $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A)/$60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less and otherwise is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Average Annual Revenue Method for ECPCs and Electing CCPCs (Subsections 127(10.31), 127(10.32), and 127(10.6)): For an ECPC (mandatory) or a single/associated CCPC that elects in prescribed form under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) (for an associated group, all member CCPCs must jointly elect), the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is reduced based on the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of the corporation (or the consolidated financial statements of the ECPC group, or the sum of average annual revenues across all associated group members regardless of whether they were associated throughout the entire 3-year period) over the preceding 3 fiscal years, beginning to phase out at $15,000,000 and becoming nil at $75,000,000 or greater3.

Short Taxation Years and Multiple Year-Ends (Subsection 127(10.5)): If a corporation has a short taxation year (or has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC), its Expenditure Limit is prorated under subsection 127(10.5) by multiplying the annual Expenditure Limit by the number of days in the short taxation year divided by 365 days3: Expenditure Limit × (number of days in the taxation year ÷ 365).

Under section 127.1 and subsection 127(5), earned SR&ED ITCs must first be applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year (Line 652 of the T2 return)3. body.text: 6.2 Deep-Dive into Major Provincial Regimes
1. Québec’s 2025–2026 Overhaul: The CRIC Regime (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T)

In the Québec Budget 2025–2026 (tabled March 25, 2025), the Québec government enacted a structural overhaul of its R&D tax system20. For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished its legacy suite of R&D tax credits—specifically (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (RD-1029.7-V), (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (RD-1029.8.6-V), (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (RD-1029.8.16.1-V), (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (RD-1029.8.9.03-V, though cumulative fee balances at the end of a post-March 25, 2025 year remain claimable for taxation years ending on or before December 31, 2029), (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, (6) the industrial design component of the In-House Design Tax Credit (retaining only the fashion design component), and (7) the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts—and consolidated them into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)20.

The CRIC is available exclusively to corporations (and corporate members of partnerships) that operate a business in Québec and maintain an establishment there (excluding individuals, trusts, and corporations claiming a large investment project tax holiday on the same property or C3i tax credit on the same asset)19. While the definition of R&D is harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) and scientifically reviewed by the CRA, the CRIC also introduces eligibility for pre-commercialization activities undertaken as a continuation of R&D carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation19. Eligible pre-commercialization work encompasses (a) tests, technological validations, and studies required to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including implementing a quality control system strictly required for initial certification), and (b) product design, including the development of form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials19.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC include: (1) 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work in Québec; (2) 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Québec; (3) 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec university entity, public research centre, or research consortium (which continue to be certified by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy); and (4) 100% of capital property acquisition costs for new depreciable assets (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings) used ≥90% in Québec for eligible activities for at least 730 consecutive days (2 years)19.

Before calculating the credit on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (version 2026-09), qualified expenditures must be reduced by an annual Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the applicable Basic Personal Amount under the Québec personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025) for each employee, prorated by the percentage of time spent by that employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities18: Exclusion Threshold = greater of $50,000 and Σ (Basic Personal Amount × percentage of the employee's time spent on eligible activities).

Unlike the prior Québec regime (where the 30% enhanced rate phased down to 14% for corporations with assets between $50 million and $75 million), the CRIC rate depends solely on the volume of spending rather than corporate asset size: it provides a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the Exclusion Threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T) and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 ceiling18. Additionally, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (unreduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold, but excluding pre-commercialization expenditures) are used to compute the Québec nexus ratio for Québec's Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI)21.

items: Ontario (OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC): Administered by the CRA, Ontario’s 8% refundable OITC (T2SCH31) applies up to a $3,000,000 expenditure limit that phases out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year Ontario taxable income and between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable paid-up capital11. The 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (T2SCH508) and refundable OBRITC (T2SCH568/T2SCH569, Section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007, which since August 9, 2007 no longer requires an advance ruling for Eligible Research Institute contracts) stack alongside the OITC56. If a corporation is in a non-taxable loss position, it may formally renounce its non-refundable ORDTC (or Manitoba non-refundable R&D credit under subsection 7.3(7) of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba)) by the federal filing due date (6 months after year-end) so that the unutilized non-refundable provincial credit does not reduce the federal Section 37 and Section 127 pools26.

British Columbia Budget 2026 Enhancements: In Budget 2026, the Government of British Columbia permanently removed the September 1, 2027 sunset date on the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666 and Schedule 5 (T2SCH5), filed within 18 months of tax year-end), restored eligibility for capital expenditures in alignment with the 2024 federal Fall Economic Statement and 2025 Federal Budget, increased refundable credit thresholds (pointing to paragraph 127(10.1)(c) of the federal Act), expanded refundable credit eligibility under section 98 to include Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, and announced exploration of a patent box regime for the life sciences sector22. Dispositions or commercial conversions of BC SR&ED property within 10 years of acquisition trigger BC recapture on Form T666 and Line 241 of Schedule 5 (sections 102.1 to 102.6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act)62.

Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG): Enacted under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020 (filing deadline 15 months after the corporation's filing due date, i.e., 21 months after tax year-end), the IEG provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's base spending level (generally the prior 2-year average) and an enhanced 20% refundable payment on incremental spending exceeding the base level, on up to $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending (phased out for taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000)11.

body.text: 3. Federal–Provincial Assistance Stacking Calculation

Because provincial R&D credits are government assistance under subsection 127(9), they reduce federal qualified expenditures on Line 513 of Form T66126. As illustrated in the benchmark stacking calculation for a CCPC in British Columbia with $1,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures12:

items: Provincial Credit (10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit): $1,000,000 × 10% = $100,00012.
Net Federal Qualified Expenditure (after provincial assistance): $1,000,000 − $100,000 = $900,00012.
Net Federal Enhanced SR&ED ITC (35% Rate): $900,000 × 35% = $315,00012.
Total Combined Cash Benefit: $100,000 + $315,000 = $415,000 (41.5% combined recovery of qualified expenditures)12.

7.1 Mandatory Prescribed Forms and the Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), 37(12), paragraph 127(9)(m), and subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act (SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, updated January 28, 2025), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing all prescribed information on or before its SR&ED reporting deadline33. The SR&ED reporting deadline is the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred33:

items: Corporations: Because corporate T2 returns are due 6 months after the end of the taxation year, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year (measured by calendar months, not a day count)33.

Individuals (Sole Proprietorships): Because T1 returns for unincorporated businesses are due June 15, the individual SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the end of the calendar taxation year33.

Partnerships: Form T661 must be filed by the partnership with its T5013 partnership information return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing due dates for the returns of income of the members for the taxation year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends (where a partnership has both individual and corporate members, the T5013 return is due on the earlier of March 31 or 5 months after fiscal period-end; if exempt from T5013 filing, partners submit the partnership Form T661 and financial statements by their respective reporting deadlines)41.
Tax-Exempt Non-Profit SR&ED Corporations (Paragraph 149(1)(j)): Must file Form T661 on or before their return filing due date to avoid late-filing penalties under subsection 149(7.1)33.

body.text: Under subsection 220(2.2), the CRA cannot by law grant any extension of time to file prescribed SR&ED forms or supply missing prescribed information after the 18-month reporting deadline expires33. If prescribed forms or prescribed fields are filed after the 18-month deadline (note: hand-delivered claims are filed on the date delivered, mailed claims on the postmark date, electronically filed T2 claims on the date the confirmation number is issued, and deadlines falling on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday extend to the next business day), the expenditures are statutorily deemed not to be SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(12) and forfeit all ITC entitlement under paragraph 127(9)(m)33. A letter expressing an "intent to file" or a claim filed with unsubstantiated estimates does not satisfy the filing requirements33. When claiming more than 20 projects in a year, a claimant may submit Part 2 technical narratives for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value at filing, provided all projects are listed in Part 6 and completed Part 2 forms for all remaining projects are kept at the claimant's place of business for immediate production upon CRA request33.
