body.text: 7.2 The Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process allows businesses to obtain upfront certainty on whether proposed R&D projects qualify technically as SR&ED before commencing work or incurring expenditures2. Applications are submitted on Form T1322 through the CRA’s My Business Account portal (with free one-on-one pre-application consultations available by emailing OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca)11.

To be eligible to apply, the taxpayer must (1) be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership, (2) have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and (3) be in good compliance standing with the CRA11. The proposed project must not have been claimed in a prior taxation year, must not involve issues currently under litigation, and must be submitted before project work begins or costs are incurred11. The CRA targets issuing a formal eligibility determination within eight (8) weeks of receiving a complete application and can approve a proposed project for a period of up to three (3) years11.

While pre-claim approval determines the technical eligibility of the proposed work and does not replace the mandatory annual filing of Form T661 and Schedule 3111, it dramatically accelerates post-filing administration: per The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), when a pre-approved project is subsequently claimed on Form T661 and selected for an expenditure-only verification review, the CRA processes the review within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim—cutting in half the standard 180-calendar-day service standard for refundable SR&ED claims selected for review2. Only if the actual work performed differs significantly from the approved proposal, or if the claim includes additional unapproved projects, will the CRA conduct a standard work-and-expenditure review on the unapproved or altered scope11.
7.3 The CRA Audit Review Process and Dispute Resolution Hierarchy

When a filed SR&ED claim is screened by the CRA’s AI-supported risk-assessment tools and the Control Function (CF) at a Coordinating Tax Services Office (CTSO) and selected for review (The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, updated April 20, 2026), the claim cannot be withdrawn because the Part 10 certification on Form T661 cannot be revoked10. The CRA targets processing refundable SR&ED claims selected for review within 180 calendar days of receiving a complete claim (90% of the time), whereas non-refundable SR&ED claims selected for review carry no fixed service standard17. Claimants are legally required under subsection 230(3) to maintain adequate technical and financial books and records (in paper or readable electronic format) for a minimum of 6 years17.

During a review, the assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) evaluates whether the claimed work meets subsection 248(1) and issues an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report (classifying reviewed work as All Work Eligible [AW], Some Work Eligible [SW], or No Work Eligible [NW]), while the Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]) audits the claimed expenditures and tax credits17. Following an initial telephone contact and written agenda/information request letter (which generally gives the claimant 30 days to provide requested pre-meeting documents), the review meeting is conducted virtually by default via videoconference (or on-site strictly on an exceptional basis) within the claimant's local business hours17. If the reviewers propose negative adjustments in a formal proposal package, the claimant is granted 30 days to submit written representations and supporting evidence17.

If disagreements arise during the review before the file is closed, the CRA’s Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (updated December 5, 2025) establish a three-step escalation protocol25:

items: Step One – Speak to the RTA and/or FR: Address factual misunderstandings or provide clarifying documentation directly to the assigned reviewers25.
Step Two – Contact the RTM and/or FRM: Escalate unresolved technical or financial disagreements to the reviewers' managers for a collaborative review of the facts and perspectives25.

Step Three – Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the formal proposal package and before the 30-day response period expires (and before the file is closed), the claimant may complete Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) and submit it to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre, which forwards the request within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director25. An Administrative Review is not a de novo technical audit; rather, the Assistant Director determines whether (a) the claimant was afforded due process (clear requests, reasonable opportunity to explain and submit evidence, and consideration of all submitted facts), and (b) the review was consistent with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, issuing a written determination of either Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered25.

body.text: Once the review is finalized and a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, a claimant that disagrees with the outcome has the statutory right under section 165 of the Income Tax Act to file a formal Notice of Objection with the Appeals Branch of the CRA, and thereafter to appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal25.
7.4 Statutory Penalties: Claim Preparer Disclosures (s. 162(5.1)) and Gross Negligence (s. 163(2))

Under subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, corporations must provide complete and accurate Claim Preparer Information in Part 9 of Form T661 (identifying any external consultant or preparer, their billing arrangement, and fees; if no external preparer assisted, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975)41. If complete and accurate claim preparer information is missing or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty applies under subsection 162(5.1), for which both the claimant corporation and the SR&ED claim preparer are jointly and severally (together or separately) liable (though an omission in Part 9 alone does not disallow the SR&ED claim itself)45. False statements in Part 9 or by third-party advisors may also trigger penalties under subsection 163(2.4) and section 163.272.

Furthermore, under subsections 163(2), 163(2)(a), 163(2)(d), 163(2.1), and 163(3) (Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy, updated January 28, 2025), if the CRA establishes on a balance of probabilities that a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (more than a simple error, oversight, or misunderstanding of the Act), made or participated in a false statement or omission on an original or amended SR&ED claim, the civil gross negligence penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of47:

items: Understated Part I Tax Payable (Paragraph 163(2)(a)): The understated Part I tax reasonably attributable to the false statement resulting from either (a) an understatement of income (note: if a disallowed SR&ED expenditure is a valid ordinary business expense deductible under the Act, disallowing it as SR&ED does not understate income; however, if a personal or fictitious expense is deducted from an overstated Section 37 pool, the CRA deems the overstated pool portion to be deducted first, and subsection 163(2.1) deems taxable income not to be less than zero in loss years), or (b) the deduction of an overstated non-refundable ITC against Part I tax payable (deemed deducted first before any valid opening, transferred, or current-year ITCs, and penalized in every carryback or carryforward year in which it is deducted)47; PLUS
Overstated Refundable ITC Claimed (Paragraph 163(2)(d)): 50% of the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the taxpayer47.

body.text: As illustrated in Section 5.2 of the CRA’s Gross Negligence Penalty Policy, if a CCPC earning the 35% enhanced ITC rate under the Proxy Method knowingly overstates directly engaged SR&ED salaries by $200,000, that false statement automatically inflates its 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount by $110,000 (55% × $200,000), overstating total qualified expenditures by $310,000, overstating the 35% ITC by $108,500 (35% × $310,000), and resulting in a $54,250 gross negligence penalty (50% × $108,500), even if net business income was not understated because the wages were deductible ordinary business expenses47.
8. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence & Audit Precedents

While CRA policies provide administrative guidance, the Federal Court of Appeal has repeatedly ruled that CRA guidelines are not binding on the courts; rather, statutory eligibility under subsection 248(1) is governed by statutory interpretation principles (Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54) and binding judicial precedent74.
8.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd., Judge Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada established the five foundational criteria—universally known as the Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Test—for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1)48:

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? In paragraph 16, Judge Bowman defined "routine engineering" as "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field"74.

Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Judge Bowman explained (at paragraph 16) that this entails a five-step process: (i) the observation of the subject matter of the problem; (ii) the formulation of a clear objective; (iii) the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (iv) the formulation of a hypothesis designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (v) the methodical and systematic testing of the hypothesis74.
Scientific Method: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?74
Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement?74
Detailed Contemporaneous Records: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results, kept as the work progressed?74

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (FCA Docket A-710-96, decided December 21, 1998, reversing [1996] T.C.J. No. 1056), the Federal Court of Appeal approved the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and emphasized that scientific research and experimental development requires repeatability and contemporaneous documentary evidence of testing79. Subsequently, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17), the Federal Court of Appeal formally summarized and adopted the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as the controlling appellate standard across Canada74.
8.3 Sass Manufacturing, 88 D.T.C. 1363 (TCC), Zeuter Development, 2006 TCC 597, and Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6

In Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 D.T.C. 1363 (TCC), and Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, 2007 D.T.C. 41, the Tax Court of Canada distinguished systematic experimental investigation from unsystematic trial-and-error adjustments and routine software development81. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (per Justice Sommerfeldt), the Tax Court reiterated that to constitute SR&ED, a project must address a technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures85. Similarly, in Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205 (at paragraph 37), the Tax Court held that "to be eligible for SR&ED, each of the questions in the five-factor test must be answered in the affirmative"78.
8.4 Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 and National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2022 FCA 72

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, 2021 D.T.C. 5050 (affirming 2019 TCC 246, per Justice Owen), and National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2022 FCA 72 (Docket A-231-20, decided May 3, 2022, per Justice Rennie, Woods and Laskin JJ.A. concurring, affirming 2020 TCC 47, per Justice Lafleur), taxpayers argued that the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test was non-binding judicial gloss or had been displaced by the CRA’s revised administrative guidelines (which removed the explicit phrase "scientific method")74.
The Federal Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed the appeal with costs in National R&D Inc. on four holdings74:

items: Binding Force of Northwest Hydraulic over CRA Guidelines: Reaffirming Kam-Press, the FCA held that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria represent the proper statutory interpretation of what Parliament intended in subsection 248(1)74. While the CRA’s 2021 guidance no longer uses the words "scientific method," "The 'How' requirement" still demands underlying rigour and discipline in the experimental process, and in any event, CRA administrative policy does not bind the courts74.

Application to Software and Applied Sciences: The FCA rejected the appellant's claim that the "engineering method" in applied sciences differs from the "scientific method," noting that any such distinction would require expert evidence at trial rather than citations to academic books of authorities, and pointing out that the Tax Court regularly recognizes eligible SR&ED in software, algorithms, databases, and precision engineering where the five criteria are met (citing Allegro Wireless Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 27; A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 48; and ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263)74.

Failure of Criteria 2 to 5 on Vague Records: Even though National R&D satisfied Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty), its claim failed Criteria 2 through 5 because its contemporaneous records were vague, unclear, conclusionary, lacked logical progression between premise and result, and showed no modification of hypotheses following testing74.

Exclusion of Non-Independent Expert Reports (Tax Court Rule 145 & White Burgess): The FCA upheld the trial judge's exclusion of the appellant's expert report because it violated section 145(2) of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) and the Code of Conduct for Experts, lacked threshold independence and impartiality under White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23 (as the appellant had authored 65% of the report and it adopted an advocacy tone), and improperly opined on how the law applied to the facts74.

body.text: 8.5 Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2023 TCC 35 and Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175

In Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2023 TCC 35 (decided March 24, 2023, per Justice Guy Smith), the appellant claimed SR&ED credits for jewellery mould development and piece finishing after bringing outsourced work in-house78. Justice Smith dismissed the appeal, noting that the employee performing the work had no prior knowledge of moulding prior to joining the appellant and was operating at an "apprenticeship level"—confirming that a company's internal lack of familiarity or apprenticeship learning curve does not constitute objective technological uncertainty under subsection 248(1)30.

Most recently, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175 (judgment delivered from the bench at Toronto on October 21, 2026, by LeBlanc, Monaghan, and Biringer JJ.A.), the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the strict evidentiary threshold under Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies76. The Court held that presenting a credible witness at trial does not displace the Minister’s assumptions of fact regarding the five Northwest Hydraulic SR&ED criteria when the oral testimony is not backed by specific, contemporaneous evidence proving that hypotheses were formulated and systematically tested as the work progressed76.
9. Comprehensive Audit & Compliance Verification Checklist

To ensure complete statutory compliance with the modernized 2025–2026 federal and provincial SR&ED regime and withstand CRA technical (RTA) and financial (FR) reviews, claimants and auditors should execute the following nine-stage verification checklist11:

cells: • Confirm the taxation year-end and the strict 18-month corporate reporting deadline (17.5 months for individuals) under subsection 37(11)11. • Verify corporate status as a CCPC or an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 20243. • For eligible businesses with gross business income under $25,000,000, evaluate submitting optional Form T1322 (Pre-Claim Approval) via My Business Account before starting work or incurring costs to secure an 8-week upfront technical determination and a 90-day post-filing expenditure review standard2.

• Frame each project in Part 2 of Form T661 (Lines 242, 244, 246) around the Two Requirements ("Why" and "How") and the Five Northwest Hydraulic Criteria11. • Compile dated, contemporaneous records generated as the work progressed proving hypothesis formulation, systematic testing, and hypothesis modification to satisfy RIS-Christie, National R&D (2022 FCA 72), and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175)74. • Establish project boundaries separating paragraph 248(1)(d) support work from paragraphs (e)–(k) excluded work and remove excess or commercial production costs from shop-floor ED+EP and ED+CP runs11.

• Compare the Traditional Method (Line 162) and the Proxy Method (Line 160) before filing Form T661, noting that the election is irrevocable for that filed taxation year under subsection 37(10)5. • Under the Proxy Method, verify the 55% PPA calculation in Part 5 (Regulation 2900(4)), strip out all universal exclusions on Line 812 (bonuses, profit-based remuneration, section 6 taxable benefits, Line 310 prior-year unpaid wages, and related benefits under Regulation 2900(9)), and verify the Overall PPA Cap (A − B − C) under Regulation 2900(6)34.

• Identify all specified employees (≥10% shareholders of any class or non-arm's-length employees under s. 248(1))37. Exclude 100% of specified employee bonuses and profit-based remuneration (s. 37(9)), apply the 5 × YMPE cap on Line 305 ($356,500 in 2025; $373,000 in 2026; shared via Form T1174 under s. 37(9.1)–(9.2)), and apply the lesser of 75% total eligible salary or 2.5 × YMPE cap ($178,250 in 2025; $186,500 in 2026) in Boxes 850–860 (Regulation 2900(7)–(8))31. • Exclude any accrued wages (Line 315, s. 78(4)) or current expenditures (Line 520, s. 127(26)) unpaid 180 days after tax year-end4. • Confirm permissible foreign SR&ED wages (Lines 307/309) meet all 5 employee/residency/nexus conditions and do not exceed 10% of domestic SR&ED wages (s. 37(1.5))1.

• Verify that all claimed capital properties were acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (s. 37(1)(b), s. 127(11.2))8. • For ASA (≥90%) depreciable property, claim on Line 390, list top 10 per project on Lines 262–263 and top 20 overall in Part 6B (Boxes 780–786), exclude from Schedule 8 (T2SCH8), and deduct any used property on Line 530 (ITR s. 2902(b))8. • For new equipment used primarily (>50% to <90%) for SR&ED (excluding GPOEF and Regulation 2900(11) PDPs), claim 25% First Term SUE and 25% Second Term SUE on Line 504 and Part 6C (Boxes 788–792) while depreciating capital cost on Schedule 813. • Claim post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs on Line 350 (100% if ASA ≥90%) and Line 355 (50% under Proxy Method if >50% to <90%, excluding GPOEF) or Line 360 (proportional under Traditional Method) and reconcile in Part 6A7.

• Confirm arm's-length contractors (Line 340) are Canadian taxable suppliers (deduct non-taxable supplier portions on Line 528) and apply the 80% inclusion rate (Line 529) to Line 340 contracts and Line 370 third-party payments (Form T1263)1. • For NAL contracts (Line 345), execute Form T1146 if transferring qualified expenditures to the payer (Line 508), and adjust NAL goods/services to cost on Lines 542–543 (s. 127(11.6))4. • Reduce pools by all government assistance (NRC IRAP, provincial R&D credits, GST/HST input tax credits on capital assets) and contract payments on Lines 429–432 and Lines 513–517 (adding the PPA portion of provincial credits to Schedule 1 income under s. 12(1)(x))26.

• Model the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit phase-out ($15M to $75M) on Schedule T2SCH31 (May 2026 version) under both prior-year taxable capital (s. 127(10.2)) and 3-year average annual gross revenue (s. 127(10.31)/(10.6)) and allocate among associated CCPCs via Schedule T2SCH49 (May 2026 version)3.

• Calculate and claim applicable provincial/territorial credits: Québec CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, 30% on first $1M above exclusion threshold / 20% excess, including pre-commercialization and capital assets for tax years beginning after March 25, 2025), Ontario (OITC 8%, ORDTC 3.5% on T2SCH508, OBRITC on T2SCH568/569), British Columbia (Form T666, 10% permanent credit including ECPCs and capital), Alberta IEG (8% base / 20% incremental up to $4M), and Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon credits18.

• Reconcile Form T661 (May 2026 version) and Schedule T2SCH31 to T2 Schedule 1 (Lines 118 and 411), Schedule 8, and financial statements11. • Audit Part 9 Claim Preparer Information for 100% accuracy to avoid the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty under subsection 162(5.1), verify all refundable ITC numbers against subsection 163(2) gross negligence rules, and preserve organized technical and financial records for the mandatory 6-year retention period17.
